title: Bake a tray, taste, then bin
allegory: A rollout buffer is like one tray of loaves baked from today's recipe: you taste them, tweak the recipe, and bin the tray, because tasting yesterday's bread says little about today's recipe.
map: one tray of loaves baked from it
one fixed-length rollout of on-policy experience
rewards, turned into reward-to-go and advantages
tweaking the recipe from the notes
binning the tray after the tweak
discarding the buffer: its data came from the old policy

props.label: keep it... but for how long?

cap.1: A learner that improves its habits by trying things needs somewhere to keep what just happened: moves, results, how likely each move was. But only briefly.
cap.2: Policy-gradient methods like REINFORCE learn from trajectories the current policy just produced. The rollout buffer stores one fixed-length batch: observations, actions, rewards, log-probs.
cap.3: REINFORCE estimates an expectation over trajectories from π_θ itself, so its data store holds exactly one on-policy batch per update cycle, across all the vectorised environments.

cap.1: Picture a baker. Bake one tray with today's recipe, taste every loaf, tweak the recipe, then bin the tray. Tomorrow's recipe needs tomorrow's bread.
cap.2: Collect a rollout with the current policy, compute returns from it, take gradient steps, discard it, collect again with the new policy. The buffer lives for one cycle.
cap.3: Collect, compute reward-to-go and advantages, update θ, clear. Samples from π_θold would bias the gradient of J(θ) unless reweighted.

chapters.name: The tasting notes
chapters.title: one CartPole rollout (γ = 1): reward-to-go counts only what came after

cap.1: The tray's notes: what was seen, what was done, the point earned, how sure the recipe was. Each step's score counts only the points that came after it.
cap.2: Each row is a timestep. Reward-to-go G_t sums rewards from t onwards, since an action can't change the past. CartPole pays +1 per step survived, so G counts down.
cap.3: G_t = Σ_{i≥t} γ^(i−t) r_i drops terms an action can't causally influence: less variance, no bias. Stored logprobs let you form importance weights against the collecting policy.

cap.1: The recipe tweak is an average over bread baked with this exact recipe. Change the recipe and the old tray came from a different bakery.
cap.2: The gradient is an expectation under the current policy. After one update, the buffer's data came from an older policy, so reusing it naively gives a biased gradient.
cap.3: ∇J(θ) = E over τ ~ π_θ of Σ G_t ∇log π_θ(a_t|s_t). Samples from π_θold need importance weights π_θ/π_θold; ARENA detaches and optionally clips them, the seed of PPO's surrogate.

chapters.name: Tray or freezer?

right.title: replay buffer
lines: a big pile of old experience

chapters.verdict: On-policy learners bin the tray; off-policy learners keep a freezer.

cap.1: A replay buffer is a freezer of every meal you've cooked, fine for a learner that can learn from anyone's cooking. A rollout buffer is today's tray only.
cap.2: A replay buffer keeps old off-policy data for a long time (DQN); a rollout buffer holds only the current on-policy batch and is thrown away (REINFORCE, PPO).
cap.3: Q-learning's max makes its update independent of the behaviour policy, which is what licenses replay. Policy gradients estimate an on-policy expectation, so their data expires with each update.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Clipped importance weights stretch one tray a little
PPO and RLHF run on rollout buffers

cap.1: When a chatbot is fine-tuned with this kind of RL, it bakes fresh trays of answers, scores them, updates, and bins them. The same loop.
cap.2: PPO reuses each rollout for a few epochs thanks to clipped importance weights, then discards it. RLHF on language models runs the same collect, update, discard cycle.
cap.3: On-policy data keeps the training signal tied to current behaviour. When you study or steer RL-trained models, the rollout loop is where their behaviour meets the reward.

coda.title: How stale is the tray? Move the recipe and watch the weights

params.label: how far the policy has moved since baking (logit shift)

caption.1: The tray was baked when left and right were 50/50. Drag how far the recipe has moved since: the correction needed to reuse old bread grows. Clipping caps it.
caption.2: Importance weight = new probability ÷ old probability of the stored action. At zero shift it's 1: fresh data. Far from zero the tray is stale, and clipped weights stop trusting it.
caption.3: iw = π_θ(a|s)/π_θold(a|s), detached; clipping to [1 − ε, 1 + ε] bounds how far a stale batch can push. So a rollout supports only a few gradient steps before it must be recollected.

where_else: PPO, which squeezes a few epochs out of each rollout with clipped importance weights
RLHF: generate answers with the current model, score them, update, discard, repeat
Replay buffers in DQN, the off-policy opposite that keeps old data for a long time

hamming.what: A container for one fixed-length batch of experience collected by the current policy, used for an update and then discarded.
hamming.when: In on-policy methods (REINFORCE, actor-critic, PPO and PPO-based RLHF), on every collect-and-update cycle.
hamming.why: Policy gradients are averages over the current policy's own behaviour, so data from an older policy goes stale the moment you update.

object.title: The age shelf
object.subtitle: Rows are training cycles, columns are how old the stored data is: a rollout buffer versus a replay buffer.

cap.1: Rows are training cycles, columns are how old the data is. A rollout buffer only ever holds this cycle's batch: one tower per row, at age zero.
cap.2: Rollout buffer: at every cycle, only freshly collected on-policy data exists.
cap.3: The on-policy estimator only admits samples from the current π_θ: age 0, every cycle.

cap.1: Switch to a replay buffer: old batches pile up, cycle after cycle. Learners like DQN happily train on any of them.
cap.2: Replay buffer: experience accumulates, and minibatches are sampled across all ages.
cap.3: Off-policy targets (a max over next actions) don't depend on the behaviour policy, so old data stays valid.

cap.1: Give the freezer a size limit and the oldest batches fall out first.
cap.2: A finite replay buffer evicts first in, first out.
cap.3: FIFO eviction bounds the age of data; too small a capacity drops the failure states the agent still needs.

cap.1: Back to the rollout buffer: after every update the old tray is binned, because the recipe that baked it no longer exists.
cap.2: Each update invalidates the batch, so the rollout buffer is cleared and refilled.
cap.3: After θ changes, the old batch is off-policy; without importance correction it biases the gradient.

cap.1: That's the price of on-policy learning: every update needs fresh experience. PPO squeezes a few extra updates from each tray with clipped weights.
cap.2: Sample cost is the trade-off; PPO reuses each rollout for a few epochs with clipped importance ratios.
cap.3: Clipped ratios bound how far a stale batch can move the policy, trading a little bias for sample reuse.

predict.q: After a policy-gradient update, why not keep training on the same rollout forever?

options.t: It came from the old policy, so the gradient estimate becomes biased
The buffer runs out of memory

predict.why: The gradient is an average over the current policy's behaviour; old data describes a policy that no longer exists.

predict.q: Which learner can happily train on a big pile of old experience?
predict.why: Q-learning's update doesn't depend on who collected the data; REINFORCE's does.

predict.q: What does reward-to-go at step t count?

options.t: Only rewards from step t onwards

predict.why: An action can't change rewards that came before it, so counting them only adds noise.
